Updated request scope as of 5/17/24 refinement sent by Mr.Small:

We have put some thought into search restrictions and terms and here is what we would suggest:

(1) total time range of January 1, 2023 through July 31, 2023
(2) Anything that includes Juli Beth Hinds, Dr. Amy Lerner, urban studies and planning (USP), global policy & strategy (GPS), UCSD in conjunction with any of those terms
(3) Anything related to the regional water equity report or RDF
(4) Anything containing a reference to "Juli Beth Hinds, Dr Amy Lerner,  Geosyntec, USP, GPS, or the RWER or RDF", UCSD in conjunction with any of those terms sent to or from "Elise Ruiz, anyone at Murakawa Communications, anyone at Geosyntec including but not limited to Ken Susillo, Megan Otto, Stephanie Zinn; and anyone at the County including but not limited to Stephanie Gaines, Crystal Benham, Todd Snyder, Sarah Agassi, Eden Brukman, and Murtaza Baxamusa"

Original Request:

To Whom it may Concern:
I am writing on behalf of my client Juli Beth Hinds. On behalf of Ms. Hinds, please consider this a formal request pursuant to California Public Records Act, Government Code §6250 et seq. for copies of all DOCUMENTS of the County of San Diego Land Use & Environment Group that reference or relate to: Juli Beth Hinds; the Department of Urban Studies and Planning at the University of California San Diego; or Nathan Fletcher. ("DOCUMENTS" as used herein, shall be defined to mean any ''writing'' as that term is defined in Evidence Code section 250, including, but not limited to, correspondence, emails, texts, communications of any kind, recordings, tapes, computer print-outs, records, slides, photographs, notes, working papers, written analyses, memoranda, plans, telegraphs, telexes and transcriptions, electronic data, and notes or memoranda made by any telephone communications.) This request encompasses all DOCUMENTS dated or created between the dates of January 1, 2022 through the date of this letter.
I request delivery of these records to our firm's office, located at 402 W. Broadway, Suite 1270, San Diego, CA 92101, or we can arrange to pick them up at a reasonable location designated by the County.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

emails.subject: [External] Harmony Grove
emails.body:
I just heard that you got that Harmony Grove development approved.  And without due consideration to traffic flow.  I understand you were somehow in charge of this project at the county?
   Yes, I read what you wrote.  But filling a page with words is very different from thinking first and writing useful information down.  You guys did not think.  And you did not go out and look at the real world.  I know you didn't because you said nothing about Via Rancho Parkway.  And a large percentage of the commuters from your new development are going to use Via Rancho Parkway to access I15.  How could you not see that?  It is already happening.
   A few years ago Citracado Parkway was widened from Auto Park down to West Valley Parkway.  So now a lot of people decided that they have a shortcut to bypass the truly awful 79 to I15 interchange during the rush hours.  They use the new Citracado Parkway.  But what happens when they get to West Valley Parkway?  The rest of Citracado does not go through to I15.  So they go west on West Valley Parkway, turn left on Via Rancho Parkway, and access I15 via that route.  I'm serious.  Since the northern part of Citracado opened, the traffic on Via Rancho Parkway has become truly awful.  Some people with driveways on that road, or who live on cross streets without street lights are effectively trapped in their homes for five hours a day.  Emergency vehicle access is almost non-existent during the busy rush "hours".  (Usually 2 or 3 hours morning and night.)  And now more people are pouring onto or off of I15 at the notoriously bad Via Rancho Parkway on ramp, which increases an already dangerous situation.
   Now, given that you din't think or look at the real world, I assume you probably have no idea what Via Rancho Parkway is like.  So let me tell you it would be REALLY expensive to widen so that it can handle the traffic that is currently being dumped onto it and the added traffic that your new development will dump onto it.  It is in rough country and would require significant excavation, retaining walls, culverts, and probably lots of eminent domain taking of land to make it work.  In short, it won't ever happen.
   So you have doomed people to die in traffic accidents or in their homes while awaiting emergency services due to your poor planning.  (And to the poor planning of whoever thought it was a good idea to finish only the one section of Citracado Parkway.)  Of course you will deny it, but you have.
   Now is there anything that can be done to mitigate the damage?  I think it's obvious:  put Citracado Parkway the rest of the way through to I15.  Go look at it.  You can do it on Google Earth if you don't want to leave your chair.  It is platted all the way through.  And it exists all the way through except for a very short stretch where it just stops abruptly.
   Look at this picture:

   The red arrow shows the end of the north section of Citracado.  Notice that the road is all widened and ready to use to that point.  The orange arrow shows the intersection on I15 that is called "Citracado Parkway".  It is there and ready to use.  The wobbly blue line that I drew shows where it appears to me that the road is supposed to continue on, eventually connecting to Gamble Lane, which I assume would then take the name Citracado as it becomes Citracado again when it passes beneath I15.  And if you look at where the yellow arrow is pointed, it looks like some clearing has even been done along this slightly curving route, though long enough ago that someone has planted a tree in the middle of it.
   Everything is in place to have Citracado extended through to I15.  So what can you do to help make that happen?  I'm sorry if you think I've been mean, but you didn't think, you did not do your due diligence, and you have created an even bigger problem than we already have by allowing this housing development.  I really do believe that people will crash and probably die due to this decision.  Or will die in their homes because emergency vehicles cannot get to them in a timely manner.  (Lest you think I'm exaggerating, it appears that my neighbor just died yesterday evening, even after calling an ambulance.  A lot of old people live off of Via Rancho Parkway.)  I think you owe it to us to at least try to mitigate the problem.

--Brian M. Godfrey
  brian@wildbirdshop.com <mailto:brian@wildbirdshop.com>

Subject: Announcement: Welcome Bethany Facendini, OSEJ GPM Community Engagement

Greetings All,

I am thrilled to introduce Bethany Facendini, our new Community Engagement and Outreach Manager for the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). Bethany is an experienced community organizer and sustainability advocate, and she will lead our efforts to engage and empower diverse communities throughout our region for climate action.

Bethany will develop and implement strategies to foster community connections and participation in environmental justice and sustainability initiatives. She will work closely with community benefit organizations, leaders, practitioners, and residents to create opportunities for collaboration and partnership.

Bethany brings a wealth of experience and expertise to OSEJ, including numerous community engagement roles in the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond, most recently with Sonoma County Regional Parks as the Community Engagement Division Manager. There, she directed marketing, communications, and cross-sector partnerships, as well as created sustainability and equity-based programs for diverse audiences, community needs assessments, and evaluation systems. In addition, Bethany helped increase the number of culturally relevant programs for under-represented populations (BIPOC, youth impacted by systems, people with disabilities, and families with low incomes). She also served as Sonoma County Human Services’ Community Engagement Manager where she led community programs to increase awareness of services and community outreach events; cultivated relationships between private, governmental, and non-profit organizations to improve partnerships; and built community networks to connect marginalized groups to programs and services. From 2013 – 2015 as the Community Engagement Coordinator for the Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Bethany worked on community engagement and outreach to advance health equity systems change initiatives. She has a Master of Arts in Environmental and Social Justice and a Bachelor of Arts degree in English and LGBTQ Studies. She also has an Urban Environmental Education Certification from Cornell University.

Bethany has world travel and living abroad experience in 46 countries, mostly economically developing nations, and recently returned from a year-long sabbatical traveling solo around the world.

FYI…

Hello Roberta, I hope all is well!  I wanted to share this announcement with you. We are sharing with our Tribal contacts, but if can help us spread the word and encourage folks to attend and submit their input, that would be greatly appreciated!  This would be the time for Tribes and those who work with Tribes to give input on what this funding should cover--for example, should it cover facilities that accommodate after school programs, pre-schools, childcare centers (which many times also serve as preschools), head start programs, etc. Many of our local tribes have these types of facilities and not necessarily official schools and it would be great if they could also use these funds to improve those indoor environments. Rehabbing those buildings would be key in improving environmental health and eliminating some of the sources of indoor air pollution <https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2022-05/IAQ-One-Page-Flyer-Final-508c.pdf>  that lead to health disparities in tribal communities.

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The graywater focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule. Stephanie
